display.title: Episode 478: The Three Sacks of Gold (Lag BaOmer)
display.summary_short: After Lag BaOmer, Uncle Yossi speaks of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the greatest blessing, Moshiach; then a story about three artists, a king's prize and a clever trick with a mirror.
display.summary_long: Broadcast just after Lag BaOmer, 5751. Uncle Yossi explains that Lag BaOmer is the yahrzeit of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, whose resting place in Meron draws Jews from all over the world to pray. In this year of wonders, the greatest blessing to ask for is Moshiach, which includes every other blessing: the sick will be healed, the world will be at peace, evil will be gone, the third Beis HaMikdash will come down from Heaven and the tzaddikim will return to life. With Sefirah's restriction lifted, the family Hakochainik march returns. A yeshiva student recites the Shema, and everyone gives tzedakah before prayer. Before Shavuos, Uncle Yossi teaches that good character comes before Torah, and tells a story about honesty: a king hires three artists to paint the walls of a room for three sacks of gold. Two work hard for thirty days, but the third arrives on the last day with a covered surprise and claims the best prize through a clever trick, until the king teaches him a wise lesson. The show ends with Shabbos candle-lighting times.
display.lesson: You can only be rewarded for your own effort: work hard, and never claim credit for the work of others.

date.note: Just after Lag BaOmer in the 'year of wonders' (5751); Shabbos candles 7:43 and Shabbos ends 8:48 fit Friday 10 May 1991 in New York; the Tuesday before is 7 May.

segments.title: Lag BaOmer and the Greatest Blessing
segments.summary: At Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's resting place in Meron, Jews pray for Moshiach, the blessing that includes all others.

segments.title: Good Character Comes Before Torah
segments.summary: Before Shavuos we learn Pirkei Avos, because good character must come before Torah.

segments.title: The Three Sacks of Gold
segments.summary: Three artists compete for a king's prizes, and the one who did nothing learns that you cannot be paid for others' work.
